newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU upbeat on 1997 economy, cautious on deficits.
newsitem.headline: EU upbeat on 1997 economy, cautious on deficits.

text.p: The European Commission said on Thursday it expected the European Union's economy to show solid signs of growth in 1997 but warned that doubts over cleaning up government budgets could undermine the rosy outlook.

In its annual economic report, the EU executive also told governments that one-off measures to meet the requirements of a single currency would not help the objective of sustainable budgetary discipline.

"The main risk to the broadly favourable outlook would seem to reside in the possible emergence of doubts on the determination of governments to accomplish the process of budgetary consolidation," the report said.

The lengthy document, which included assessments of each member of the 15-nation bloc, did not include new forecasts for growth in the EU or expectations for budget deficits. These will come in late April or early May.
But the Commission reaffirmed its expectation of a rebound in growth in 1997 and 1998.

"Output growth is expected to pick up to around trend rate in 1997 and above its trend in 1998," the Commission said. During its last forecasting exercise in the autumn, growth in the EU was seen rising by 2.3 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998.
Worries are resurfacing over the ability of several large countries, notably Germany, to meet the strict conditions of economic and monetary union (EMU).

With unemployment in Germany at its highest level since the 1930s, economists have begun to question whether Bonn can bring its 1997 budget deficit down to 3.0 percent of output, the Maastricht target.

Long viewed as a paragon of fiscal virtue, Germany finds itself facing an uncomfortable dilemma as it continues to argue for a strict reading of the Maastricht criteria on deficits, inflation and interest rates.

While this stand is often justified on the grounds of establishing a credible common currency, it has also been seen in some quarters as an attempt to keep countries like Italy out of the first wave of EMU participants.
Economists say the irony of this hardline stance is that it might come back to haunt Germany itself.
Regarding Italy, the Commission said that low interest rates and robust growth were key elements in Rome's attempts to qualify for monetary union.
But discussing some governments' tactics to cut expenditure, the Commission said that one-off efforts would not help the process of long-lasting budgetary rigour.
"It is evident that the temporary nature of these (types of) measures does not contribute to improving the fundamental budget situation," the report says.
The EU will next week announce its opinion on several budgetary practices governments have used to bring their deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product.
One of the more controversial proposals is Italy's euro tax, a one-time revenue raising measure that some have criticised as being at odds with durable budgetary convergence.
Countries must bring their deficits, inflation and interest rates in line with the Maastricht treaty this year if they hope to qualify for monetary union, expected to start in 1999.
